messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault happened on a Tuesday in November, when the humidity had given way to a brittle cold. At twenty-six, Elias had come home to find his girlfriend drinking heavily, her breathing shallow and erratic. When he reached for her arm to guide her to the couch, the alcohol smell hit him first, sharp and cloying. She shoved him backward. He struck his head against the drywall, hearing a sickening crack before his vision swam. What followed was a blur of strikes and kicks, the wet thud of his own ribs against the floorboards, the copper taste of blood pooling under his tongue. He lay there until she finally threw a ceramic mug against the wall and stormed into the bedroom, leaving him with a split lip, a purple bruise blooming across his collarbone, and a wave of nausea so violent he retched into the hallway rug. He fled the apartment that night, but the trauma did not stay behind. Within weeks, the precinct coffee machine became a minefield. Every time the barista frothed milk over the distinct, yeasty scent of spent beer, Elias felt his stomach drop, a sudden wave of nausea mirroring the one on his floorboards. That physical lurch did not pass unnoticed; it pulled the assault into sharp focus, his mind replaying the crunch of the mug shattering and his own desperate pleas with perfect, unfiltered clarity. The memories refused to sit quietly. They forced their way into his focus during roll call, vivid and uncontrolled, stripping away any distance between past and present. As the sensory echoes of that night multiplied, so did his conviction that the world had fundamentally shifted. He began to see every interaction through the lens of sudden violence. The smell of stale drinks in break rooms, the sight of a colleague’s bruised knuckles from a basketball game, even a raised voice in the hallway—all of it confirmed a new, rigid belief that people are never as they appear and that he is permanently an outsider in his own life. That isolation, in turn, acted as fuel for the intrusions. Because Elias had come to believe that no one could be trusted and that safety was an illusion, his brain stopped filtering out threat. The negative appraisal that he was permanently on the outside made the traumatic memories feel more urgent, more real, and impossible to dismiss. The uncontrolled access to those vivid, sensory-laden recollections then dictated his daily behavior. He stopped trying to process what happened, opting instead to shut down completely. He began to emotionally numb himself, treating his feelings as liabilities rather than signals. When his wife, Sarah, reached out to hold him after a hard shift, he would stiffen and step back, avoiding being touched because any physical contact felt like the prelude to violence. He also refused to relax, lying awake on the couch with the television blaring or pacing the floors, convinced that letting his guard down was dangerously close to being caught off guard again. These defensive habits quickly calcified into a self-reinforcing trap. By consistently avoiding relaxation and cutting himself off emotionally, Elias found himself increasingly isolated from his wife and his partner’s support network. This withdrawal cemented his belief that he was an outsider, reinforcing the distrust that had kept him in survival mode. He was certain that the emotional numbing meant to protect him instead left his nervous system chronically hyper-aroused, meaning that minor environmental shifts—like the clink of keys at the door or a heavy footstep on the stairwell—readily triggered that familiar wave of nausea and sensory flashbacks. He had tried to manage the threat by building walls, but those walls only narrowed his perception of danger, making the triggers feel omnipresent and inescapable. At work, his hyper-vigilance bled into his investigations; he started doubting the credibility of informants without cause, pushing away veterans who tried to debrief with him, and ultimately calling in sick three days in a row after a routine domestic dispute call left him frozen in the squad car, unable to speak. What finally brought Elias to my office was the night Sarah left his keys on the counter and walked out, telling him she could not live with a ghost. He realized the numbness and avoidance were not shielding him from the past but erasing his present. He now sits across from me, hands folded tightly in his lap, bracing for the next intrusion while quietly hoping that therapy might teach him how to stop bracing. He fears that if he finally lets go of the hyper-vigilance, the nausea and the memories will overwhelm him completely, but he is desperate to find a way back to a life where he is not waiting for the next blow.
